analysis.one_liner: Requires federally funded construction to be built above projected flood levels using current climate science.
analysis.headline: Sponsored with two cosponsors in May 2021, the bill sat in the Senate Banking Committee without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write the 2015 Federal Flood Risk Management Standard into law. Federal agencies would have to design, build, and finance projects well above the current base flood elevation — two feet higher for ordinary projects, three for critical facilities like hospitals — using climate-informed flood data, consider alternatives to building in floodplains, and tell state, local, and tribal governments and the public before building in a floodplain. Agencies guaranteeing or insuring loans in flood-prone areas would have to warn the private parties involved about the hazard. It died in committee without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live and work near rivers and coasts, and federal taxpayers generally. The federal government repeatedly pays to rebuild flood-damaged projects it financed to an outdated standard; this bill would require new federally funded construction to account for current and future flood risk up front. Communities would get notice and a chance to comment before a federal project goes into their floodplain, and borrowers in flood zones would be warned of the hazard before completing a federally backed transaction.

how_it_helps.text: Agencies must design federally funded projects using a climate-informed science approach and add 2 feet (3 for critical facilities) of elevation above the base flood, so projects last as long as intended instead of flooding early.

Before building in a floodplain, agencies must consider alternatives, prefer natural flood protections, and send state, local, and tribal governments a short notice with a comment period and early public review.
Any agency that guarantees, approves, regulates, or insures a financial transaction in a base-flood area must inform participating private parties of the hazards before completing the action.
Agencies must report on how the requirements affect their operations, and the Water Resources Council must update the standard at least every five years as flood science changes.

analysis.who_pays: Federal agencies and the contractors and developers building with federal money would face higher design and construction costs — elevating structures, floodproofing, and extra review steps — plus some added delay from notices and comment periods. Projects in floodplains would cost more up front than under the old standard.
analysis.who_pays_short: Developers and contractors on federally funded projects

drawbacks.text: Higher elevation and climate-based design standards raise the up-front cost of federally funded construction, and the notice and comment requirements add procedural steps and time.

The exemptions are broad: an agency head can waive the standard for national security, emergencies, or whenever applying it is 'demonstrably inappropriate,' giving agencies considerable discretion to skip the requirements.

The bill only covers federally funded projects and federal actions; it does not require private development outside federal programs to build to the higher standard, so much new floodplain construction would remain at the old elevation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade is modest added construction cost and paperwork against avoided flood losses. Federal projects built to the old base-flood standard have repeatedly needed expensive rebuilding after floods, so designing for projected flood levels tends to pay for itself over a project's life. The bill's weak points are its broad waiver authority and its limited reach — it leaves purely private floodplain development untouched. On balance the design is reasonable, though the exemptions could swallow the rule in practice.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee never took the bill up — no hearing, no markup, no vote — so it never reached the floor before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Chris Van Hollen introduced the bill on May 18, 2021, joined by Sens. Schatz and Booker.
The bill was read twice and referred the same day to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
No further action appears in the record: the committee never held a hearing or vote, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
The bill would have codified the 2015 Federal Flood Risk Management Standard, a flexible framework requiring agencies to plan for current and future flood risk on federally funded projects.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Developers and contractors building in floodplains with federal money keep the lower design standard, and federal taxpayers keep absorbing the cost of rebuilding flood-damaged projects that were financed without future flood risk in mind.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Floodplain developers; taxpayers still bear flood losses

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Democrats and the committee, which never acted, was chaired by a Democrat; no vote or recorded opposition exists, so the partisan shape of the opposition cannot be measured.

industries.industry: Homebuilders and developers building in floodplains with federal funds
industries.note: The bill would raise their design and construction costs by requiring elevation above projected flood levels and extra review on federally funded projects. Their lower costs under the status quo come largely at taxpayers' expense, since the government pays to rebuild projects that flood.
They would face stricter specifications and added documentation on federal jobs, but projects designed for future flood levels are less likely to need costly rebuilding and litigation later.

industries.industry: Property and flood insurers (including the National Flood Insurance Program)
industries.note: Fewer flood-damaged structures built at outdated elevations means fewer claims and less federal flood insurance exposure. The bill also requires federal lenders and insurers to warn buyers about flood hazards.
